setting_note: In a rural hospital where the chart may be the only record seen by the visiting anaesthetist and surgeon, an accurate adverse drug reaction section completed in clinic matters even more; the GP summary should be updated as well.

references.title: National Inpatient Medication Chart user guide
references.locator: Adverse drug reactions and allergies section: required information

references.title: National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards: Medication Safety Standard
references.locator: Documentation of medicines-related information including adverse drug reactions

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Antimicrobial hypersensitivity: assessing and documenting penicillin allergy

tutor_context: Key facts: the adverse drug reaction section must be completed before prescribing; it records drug, reaction, type (allergy or intolerance), date and source, with signature; an empty section is not the same as no known reactions; a red alert band is applied where a reaction is recorded. Penicillin allergy labels should be clarified (nature, timing, severity) because many are low risk and can be delabelled. Misconceptions: omitting intolerances, upgrading reactions to anaphylaxis, or leaving the section blank. Out of scope: formal penicillin allergy testing pathways.
plan: Tests recall of what must be documented in the adverse drug reaction section of the medication chart, evidencing outcomes 1.8, 1.1 and 1.10. The rural preadmission clinic with an elderly patient and an incomplete GP summary makes the task realistic. Distractors are omitting an intolerance, exaggerating the reaction and recording no known allergies. Supported by the ACSQHC National Inpatient Medication Chart user guide.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide. A 52-year-old Aboriginal man with well-controlled type 2 diabetes presents with 2 days of a warm, red, tender area over his left shin after a scratch while fencing. There is no abscess, ulcer or necrosis, the erythema is 8 cm across and marked, and he has no fever; heart rate 84, blood pressure 132/80, blood glucose 7.1 mmol/L. He has no history of MRSA infection and the local antibiogram shows low community MRSA rates; he has no drug allergies. He lives 40 minutes away, has transport and would like to go home. The GP on call agrees with discharge and asks you to prescribe oral antibiotics and arrange review with the Aboriginal health service in 48 hours.
lead_in: Which antibiotic prescription is most appropriate?

options.text: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid 875 mg with 125 mg orally twice daily for 10 days
Flucloxacillin 500 mg orally 6-hourly for 5 days, extended if slow to resolve
Cefalexin 500 mg orally 6-hourly for 14 days to cover his diabetes
Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole 160 mg with 800 mg orally twice daily for 7 days

explanations.A: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is broader than needed for uncomplicated cellulitis, which is almost always caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus, and a 10-day course exceeds the recommended duration.
explanations.B: Mild cellulitis without systemic features is treated with an oral anti-staphylococcal penicillin; flucloxacillin (or dicloxacillin) 500 mg 6-hourly for 5 days is the Therapeutic Guidelines first-line regimen, with the course extended if improvement is slow. Marking the erythema margin and reviewing at 48 hours allows early detection of failure.
explanations.C: Cefalexin is an acceptable alternative where adherence to 6-hourly flucloxacillin is a concern, but 14 days is far longer than recommended and increases adverse effects and resistance without benefit.
explanations.D: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is used when MRSA is likely (previous MRSA, or high community prevalence); it has unreliable activity against Streptococcus pyogenes and is not first line in a patient without MRSA risk factors.

learning_point: Mild cellulitis without systemic features is treated with oral flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly for 5 days, extended only if resolution is slow, with early review rather than broader or longer therapy.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the 48-hour review can be shared with the local Aboriginal health service, which supports culturally safe follow-up and transport; a patient living remotely with no reliable review may need a lower threshold for admission or intravenous therapy, which is not the case here.
secondary_areas: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

generation.uncertainty_note: Therapeutic Guidelines durations for cellulitis have shortened over successive editions; the 5-day course with extension if slow to resolve reflects the current edition and should be verified at review.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Cellulitis and erysipelas: mild infection, oral therapy and duration

references.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Quality statements on appropriate choice and duration of antimicrobials

tutor_context: Key facts: mild cellulitis is treated orally with flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly, cefalexin if adherence is a problem, for 5 days with extension if slow to resolve; mark the margin and review at 48 hours; MRSA cover is added only with risk factors; diabetes alone does not require intravenous therapy. Misconceptions: that broader or longer courses are safer, or that Aboriginal identity in itself is an MRSA risk factor rather than local prevalence and personal history. Out of scope: diabetic foot infection, which is a different guideline.
plan: Tests choice and duration of oral antibiotics for mild cellulitis, evidencing outcomes 1.8, 1.7 and 1.3. The regional ED with a GP on call and the Aboriginal health service for follow-up shows culturally safe discharge planning. Distractors are an overly broad agent, an overly long course and MRSA-directed therapy without indication. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the medical ward of a metropolitan general hospital; the registrar is on site. A 58-year-old man was admitted 3 days ago from the emergency department with community-acquired pneumonia and was started empirically on intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam because he was initially tachycardic and febrile. Blood cultures taken before antibiotics have grown Streptococcus pneumoniae, fully susceptible to penicillin. He has been afebrile for 36 hours, is eating and drinking, has a respiratory rate of 18 on room air, and wants to go home tomorrow. On the morning round the registrar says, 'Sort out his antibiotics today' and moves to the next patient. The pharmacist has also left a note on the chart about antimicrobial stewardship.
lead_in: What is the most important action regarding his antibiotics today?

options.text: Continue intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam until he has completed 7 days, then stop
Leave the antibiotics unchanged until the consultant reviews him on tomorrow's ward round
Switch to oral amoxicillin and document a stop date for a 5 to 7 day course
Request infectious diseases approval so that piperacillin with tazobactam can be continued

explanations.A: Continuing a broad-spectrum intravenous agent when a fully susceptible organism is known and the patient has met criteria for oral switch exposes him to unnecessary adverse effects, cannula-related infection and resistance, and delays discharge.
explanations.B: Deferral for a day is not justified; de-escalation and intravenous to oral switch are expected daily actions that the junior doctor should carry out with the registrar's agreement, and the registrar has already asked for it.
explanations.C: He is clinically stable, afebrile, tolerating oral intake and has a penicillin-susceptible pneumococcus, so narrowing to oral amoxicillin and setting a total duration of 5 to 7 days is the stewardship priority; documenting the stop date on the chart ensures the course is not continued by default.
explanations.D: Seeking approval to continue a broad-spectrum agent is the opposite of what is needed; restricted antimicrobials require justification, and here there is none.

learning_point: When a susceptible organism is identified and the patient is stable and tolerating oral intake, de-escalate to the narrowest effective oral antibiotic and document a stop date.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without an on-site pharmacist or infectious diseases service, the same de-escalation is made by the junior doctor with the GP or visiting physician, using Therapeutic Guidelines and the local antimicrobial stewardship phone line.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Community-acquired pneumonia in adults: directed therapy and intravenous to oral switch; principles of antimicrobial use

references.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Quality statements on review of therapy, de-escalation and documentation of duration

tutor_context: Key facts: criteria for intravenous to oral switch include clinical improvement, haemodynamic stability, ability to absorb oral medicines and an oral option; directed therapy for penicillin-susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia is amoxicillin; total duration for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia is usually 5 to 7 days; every antibiotic order should carry an indication and review or stop date. Misconceptions: that broad agents are safer, or that courses must be completed as started. Out of scope: severity scoring at admission.
plan: Tests prioritising de-escalation and oral switch as the key antibiotic action for a stable patient with a susceptible organism, evidencing outcomes 1.8 and 1.7. The metro ward with a busy registrar and a pharmacist note makes it the junior doctor's job. Distractors are inertia, deferral and an inappropriate approval request. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are the PGY2 in the emergency department of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with specialist advice available by phone. A 60-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve presents at 21:00 after an hour of epistaxis that stopped with 20 minutes of pressure. He started a course of trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole 5 days ago for a urinary infection. He has no other bleeding, no headache, no melaena, and his observations are normal; haemoglobin is 142 g/L. His INR tonight is 7.5, with a target range of 2.5 to 3.5. The hospital pharmacy holds vitamin K and a small stock of prothrombin complex concentrate.
lead_in: What does this INR result mean for his management?

options.text: A life-threatening bleed, requiring prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K 10 mg immediately, before any transfer
An acceptable INR for a patient with a mechanical valve, requiring no change to his warfarin dosing
A supratherapeutic INR requiring warfarin to be stopped permanently and replaced with apixaban
A supratherapeutic INR with minor bleeding, needing warfarin withheld, low-dose vitamin K and an INR recheck in 24 hours

explanations.A: Full reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate and high-dose vitamin K is reserved for major or life-threatening bleeding; using it here would risk valve thrombosis and make re-anticoagulation difficult for days.
explanations.B: An INR of 7.5 is well above his target of 2.5 to 3.5 and has already caused bleeding; it must be acted on, and the interaction with trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole explains the rise.
explanations.C: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated in patients with mechanical heart valves; warfarin is withheld temporarily, not replaced.
explanations.D: An INR between 4.5 and 10 with minor bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin, giving a small dose of vitamin K (1 to 2 mg orally or intravenously) so that the INR falls without overshooting below his valve's target range, and rechecking the INR within 24 hours before deciding on dose resumption. The interacting antibiotic should be reviewed.

learning_point: An INR of 4.5 to 10 with minor bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin, low-dose vitamin K and an INR recheck within 24 hours; full reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate is only for major bleeding, especially in patients with mechanical valves.
setting_note: In a regional hospital with limited prothrombin complex concentrate stock and no on-site haematology, it is important to reserve concentrate for major bleeding and to seek telephone advice from the receiving haematology or cardiology service if there is any doubt about a mechanical valve patient.

generation.uncertainty_note: Vitamin K dose bands for INR 4.5 to 10 vary slightly between Therapeutic Guidelines and local anticoagulation protocols; the principle of low-dose vitamin K and no prothrombin complex concentrate for minor bleeding is consistent.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Warfarin: management of elevated INR and bleeding

references.title: Tran H et al., Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis consensus guidelines for warfarin reversal, Medical Journal of Australia 2013
references.locator: Recommendations by INR and bleeding severity

tutor_context: Key facts: warfarin reversal is graded by INR and bleeding: INR above target without bleeding, withhold and reduce; INR 4.5 to 10 without bleeding, withhold and consider vitamin K 1 to 2 mg; INR above 10, vitamin K 3 to 5 mg; any major bleeding, prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg with fresh frozen plasma if unavailable. Mechanical valves need cautious reversal to avoid thrombosis. Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is a major warfarin potentiator. Misconceptions: reversing fully for epistaxis, or switching valve patients to direct oral anticoagulants. Out of scope: bridging anticoagulation when restarting.
plan: Tests interpretation of a supratherapeutic INR with minor bleeding in a mechanical valve patient, evidencing outcomes 1.8, 1.5 and 1.1. The regional ED with limited concentrate stock and phone-only haematology makes the graded decision matter. Distractors are over-reversal, inaction and an inappropriate anticoagulant switch. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular and the ASTH warfarin reversal guideline.

stem: You are the only doctor overnight, covering the wards at a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula; the GP is on call at home. A 58-year-old woman, weight 70 kg, admitted 2 days ago with community-acquired pneumonia, developed a swollen right calf this afternoon. The visiting sonographer confirmed an above-knee deep vein thrombosis at 17:00. Her eGFR is 55 mL/min/1.73 m2, platelets 240 x 10^9/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L, and she has no history of bleeding, recent surgery or liver disease. The GP has reviewed her by phone, agrees she should start treatment-dose low molecular weight heparin tonight, and asks you to chart it. The nurse brings the medication chart and the ward stock of enoxaparin.
lead_in: Which prescription is most appropriate?

options.text: Enoxaparin 70 mg subcutaneously every 12 hours
Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily
Enoxaparin 70 mg subcutaneously once daily because of her reduced eGFR
Unfractionated heparin by intravenous infusion with 6-hourly APTT monitoring

explanations.A: Treatment-dose enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism is 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours (or 1.5 mg/kg once daily); for a 70 kg patient this is 70 mg 12-hourly. Her renal function (eGFR 55) does not require dose adjustment, and her platelets and bleeding risk are acceptable.
explanations.B: Forty milligrams once daily is the prophylactic dose; it is inadequate for an established above-knee deep vein thrombosis and leaves her at risk of extension and pulmonary embolism.
explanations.C: Renal dose reduction of enoxaparin (1 mg/kg once daily) applies when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min; at an eGFR of 55 full treatment dosing is used.
explanations.D: An unfractionated heparin infusion is reserved for patients with severe renal impairment, very high bleeding risk or a likely need for urgent reversal; it is harder to run safely in a small rural ward overnight and offers no advantage here.

learning_point: Treatment of venous thromboembolism with enoxaparin is 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours (or 1.5 mg/kg daily) at normal or mildly reduced renal function; dose reduction applies only when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min.
setting_note: In a rural ward overnight, subcutaneous enoxaparin is the practical choice because an unfractionated heparin infusion needs frequent APTT sampling and nursing adjustment that a single-doctor site may not support; the GP decides on transition to an oral anticoagulant in the morning.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Venous thromboembolism: initial anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Enoxaparin: treatment dose and dose adjustment in renal impairment

tutor_context: Key facts: enoxaparin treatment dose is 1 mg/kg 12-hourly or 1.5 mg/kg daily, using actual body weight; reduce to 1 mg/kg daily if creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min; prophylactic dose is 40 mg daily; check platelets and bleeding risk before starting; direct oral anticoagulants may be started instead when appropriate. Misconceptions: confusing prophylactic and treatment doses, and applying renal adjustment at mild impairment. Out of scope: choice and duration of ongoing oral anticoagulation.
plan: Tests correct weight-based treatment dosing of enoxaparin and when renal adjustment applies, evidencing outcomes 1.8 and 1.1. The single-doctor rural ward overnight with the GP by phone makes the intern the prescriber. Distractors are the prophylactic dose, unnecessary renal reduction and a heparin infusion. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular and the Australian Medicines Handbook.

stem: You are the PGY2 on the medical ward of a regional hospital without an ICU, where CT is available in business hours and patients are retrieved to Adelaide when needed. A 68-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis, who takes methotrexate 15 mg orally once weekly with folic acid, is admitted with a lower urinary tract infection and mild dehydration; he is not septic. His eGFR is 58 mL/min/1.73 m2, full blood count is normal, and he has no drug allergies. The GP covering the ward asks you to chart an oral antibiotic from the ward's standard options and to check for interactions with his regular medicines before you do.
lead_in: Which antibiotic carries the greatest risk of a serious interaction with his regular medicines?

options.text: Cefalexin
Trimethoprim
Nitrofurantoin
Amoxicillin

explanations.A: Cefalexin has no clinically important interaction with methotrexate or folic acid and is a reasonable choice for cystitis in a man when susceptibility allows.
explanations.B: Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and reduces renal clearance of methotrexate; combined with weekly methotrexate, particularly in an older patient with reduced renal function and dehydration, it can cause severe pancytopenia and mucositis. The combination should be avoided even with low-dose methotrexate.
explanations.C: Nitrofurantoin does not interact significantly with methotrexate; its main limitation is reduced efficacy and increased toxicity when creatinine clearance is well below 45 mL/min, which should be checked but is a separate issue.
explanations.D: Amoxicillin has no important interaction with methotrexate at this dose; high-dose penicillins can reduce methotrexate clearance in oncology dosing, but this is not relevant to weekly low-dose rheumatological therapy.

learning_point: Trimethoprim, alone or with sulfamethoxazole, must be avoided in patients taking methotrexate because of the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without a clinical pharmacist on every shift, the junior doctor is often the last interaction check before dispensing; the Australian Medicines Handbook and the medication safety phone line are available at all sites.

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Methotrexate: interactions (trimethoprim, sulfamethoxazole)

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Urinary tract infection: acute cystitis in men; antimicrobial choice

tutor_context: Key facts: methotrexate plus trimethoprim (with or without sulfamethoxazole) is a well-documented cause of fatal pancytopenia, amplified by renal impairment, dehydration and older age; other methotrexate interactions include NSAIDs at high dose and proton pump inhibitors in high-dose therapy; weekly methotrexate itself is a high-risk medicine requiring a clearly documented day of the week. Misconceptions: assuming low-dose methotrexate is safe with trimethoprim, or that folic acid supplementation protects against the interaction. Out of scope: antibiotic durations for cystitis in men.
plan: Tests recall of the dangerous methotrexate and trimethoprim interaction when choosing a urinary antibiotic, evidencing outcomes 1.8 and 1.1. The regional ward with the GP delegating the interaction check makes the PGY2 responsible. Distractors are the other common oral cystitis agents, none of which interact importantly. Supported by the Australian Medicines Handbook methotrexate interactions entry.
